resources.label: Learn C#
resources.note: Our C# practice site. Type each example in, run it, and change it. C# is one of the languages AQA accepts in the exam.

tips.title: Zero to LEN minus one
tips.body: An array of $n$ items runs from index **0** to **$n-1$**, so `LEN(a) - 1` is the last index, not `LEN(a)`. Say "zero to LEN minus one" out loud as you write the FOR line and the off-by-one cannot happen.

tips.title: The starting value names the pattern
tips.body: Look at what a variable is set to **before** the loop. **0** with `+ a[i]` inside is a running **total**. **0** with `+ 1` inside an IF is a **counter**. **`a[0]`** is a **largest or smallest** finder. That one glance tells you what the algorithm is for.

tips.title: Never start biggest at zero
tips.body: Set `biggest ← a[0]`, not `biggest ← 0`. With all-negative data, nothing ever beats 0 and the algorithm reports a value that is not in the array. Starting from the first item guarantees the answer is really there.

tips.title: Rows then columns, always
tips.body: A two-dimensional array is `a[row][column]` in that order. Write the row loop outside and the column loop inside, matching the order in the brackets, and the nesting writes itself.

why.matters:
Thirty marks in thirty variables cannot be looped over, searched, sorted or counted, because as far as the program is concerned `mark1` and `mark2` have nothing to do with each other. Put them in an array and the index is a **number**, so one loop reaches all thirty.

That is what a data structure buys: not storage, but the ability to treat many values as one thing. An **array** holds many of the same type; a **record** holds one each of several types; and almost every real collection of data is one of those inside the other.

examples.title: Why the thirty-first mark is not a problem
examples.body:
With thirty named variables, a thirty-first student means editing every part of the program that touches the marks. With an array, nothing changes: the loop runs from `0` to `LEN(marks) - 1`, so it handles whatever length the array happens to be.

That is the difference worth writing down. An array is not a tidier way of keeping thirty variables — it is what makes the code independent of **how many there are**. Totalling, averaging, searching and sorting are written once and then work on a list of any length.

visual.alt: A table comparing thirty separate variables with one array: totalling takes thirty lines or one loop, adding a thirty-first value means editing everywhere or nothing at all, and sorting is barely possible until the values share one name

examples.title: Why a seating plan needs two indexes
examples.body:
One row of a cinema is an array. The whole auditorium is an array **of rows** — a 2D array — and `seats[row][column]` picks a seat, both counted from 0.

Spreadsheets, chessboards and every grid of pixels are stored this way. Going through one takes a loop inside a loop: the outer one walks the rows, the inner one walks the seats in that row, and the inner loop runs completely for each single pass of the outer. That is why nested loops and 2D arrays turn up in the same question.

visual.alt: A table of lookups into a two-dimensional array of two rows of three numbers: the first row on its own, then single values picked out by row and column with both indexes counted from zero, the length of the outer array, which counts the rows, and the length of the first row, which counts the columns

examples.title: Why a student is not three arrays
examples.body:
Names in one array, ages in another, grades in a third: that works only as long as all three stay in the same order. Remove one student from two of them and the data quietly belongs to the wrong people, with nothing to say so.

A **record** holds different types together under one name — `name` a string, `age` an integer, `grade` a character — so a student is one thing that moves as one thing. An array of records is then a table: one record per row, one field per column, which is exactly how a database holds it.

visual.alt: A table of one student record with four fields of different types: a name held as a string, an age as an integer, a grade as a single character and whether they have paid as a Boolean

steps.title: An array is a numbered list
steps.body:
An **array** holds many values of the **same type** under one name. Each value has an **index**, and indexes **start at 0**.

```
scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]
OUTPUT scores[0]
OUTPUT scores[3]
OUTPUT LEN(scores)
```

Output: `12`, `15`, `4`. The first item is index 0, the last is index 3, and `LEN` gives the number of items, which is always one more than the last index.

You can change an item too: `scores[1] ← 20` replaces the 7, so the array becomes `[12, 20, 9, 15]`.

visuals.alt: The array scores as a table: index 0 holds 12, index 1 holds 7, index 2 holds 9, index 3 holds 15

steps.title: Visiting every item
steps.body:
To do something with every item, loop over the indexes from `0` to `LEN(array) - 1`. This is called **traversing** the array. Using `LEN` means the code works however long the array is.

```
scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]
total ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(scores) - 1
   total ← total + scores[i]
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```

Output: `43`.

AQA also has `FOR value IN scores … ENDFOR`, which visits every element without indexes. You cannot change the array's items that way, so use the indexed loop when you need to write to it.

visuals.alt: Trace of the total program: i runs 0 to 3, total goes 12, 19, 28, 43

check.prompt: What would happen if the loop ran `FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(scores)` instead?
check.solution: Index 4 is one past the end. This off-by-one error is the commonest array bug.
options: It would add the total twice, because the last pass repeats the final item before the loop ends
On the last pass it would try to read scores[4], which does not exist, and the program would crash or give an error
It would work the same, because LEN is the last index and the loop would simply stop at the final item
It would skip the first item, because the loop would start counting from the wrong end of the array

steps.title: Finding the largest value
steps.body: A standard pattern: start `biggest` at the first item, then loop from index 1, replacing `biggest` whenever a larger value turns up.

visuals.problem: Find the largest value in scores

steps.text:
```
scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]
biggest ← scores[0]
FOR i ← 1 TO LEN(scores) - 1
   IF scores[i] > biggest THEN
      biggest ← scores[i]
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT biggest
```
7 and 9 are not bigger; 15 is, so biggest becomes 15

visuals.alt: Trace of the biggest program: biggest starts at 12; i 1 gives 7, not bigger; i 2 gives 9, not bigger; i 3 gives 15, which is bigger, so biggest becomes 15

check.prompt: To find the smallest value instead, which one change is needed?
check.solution: Same pattern, opposite comparison. Starting at 0 would just compare the first item with itself.
options: Change > to < in the IF
Start biggest at 0
Start the loop at 0 instead of 1
Use LEN(scores) instead of LEN(scores) − 1

steps.title: Two-dimensional arrays
steps.body:
A **2D array** is a grid: an array of arrays. `grid[row][column]`, both from 0.

```
grid ← [[3, 8, 1],
        [5, 2, 7]]
OUTPUT grid[1][2]
OUTPUT grid[0][1]
```

Output: `7` then `8`. `LEN(grid)` is the number of rows, 2, and `LEN(grid[0])` is the length of the first row, 3, which is the number of columns. A cell is updated the same way it is read: `grid[1][1] ← 9` changes the 2 to a 9 and leaves every other cell alone.

To visit every cell, use **nested loops**: the outer loop picks the row, the inner loop walks along it. For 2 rows and 3 columns the inner loop runs 3 times for each of 2 rows: 6 cells.

visuals.alt: The 2D array grid: row 0 is 3, 8, 1 and row 1 is 5, 2, 7

visuals.problem: Output every cell of grid, row by row

steps.text:
```
FOR r ← 0 TO LEN(grid) - 1
   FOR c ← 0 TO LEN(grid[0]) - 1
      OUTPUT grid[r][c]
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
```
Outer loop: rows, up to LEN(grid) − 1. Inner loop: columns, up to LEN(grid[0]) − 1, so the same code works for a grid of any size

check.prompt: With the grid above, what is `grid[0][2] + grid[1][0]`?

steps.title: Records: different types together
steps.body:
An array holds one type. A **record** groups **different types** under one name, each in a named **field**. A student has a name (string) and an age (integer); a record keeps them together.

```
RECORD Student
   name : String
   age : Integer
ENDRECORD

s ← Student('Mia', 15)
OUTPUT s.name + ' is ' + INT_TO_STRING(s.age)
```

Output: `Mia is 15`. Fields are reached with a dot: `s.name`. You update a field the same way: `s.age ← 16` changes just that field and leaves `s.name` alone. An **array of records** is how a program stores a whole class: `pupils[4].age` is the age of the fifth pupil.

An array of records is built the same way as any other array:

```
pupils ← [Student('Mia', 15), Student('Jon', 16), Student('Ada', 15)]
OUTPUT pupils[1].name
```

Output: `Jon`.

visuals.problem: Why not use two arrays, names and ages?

steps.text: With two arrays, names[3] and ages[3] belong together only by luck of the index
Sort one array and the other no longer matches
A record keeps each student's values together, so they cannot come apart

check.prompt: `pupils` is an array of `Student` records. Write the expression for the name of the first pupil.

steps.title: Your turn: counting with a condition
steps.body:
Write code that counts how many values in `temps` are above 19. Plan: a counter set to 0, a loop over every index, an IF inside that adds 1 when the test is true.

Then build the same thing on our [Learn C#](https://red-dune-0f7372e10.7.azurestaticapps.net/) site with an `int[]` and a `foreach` loop, and run it.

steps.text:
```
temps ← [18, 21, 19, 23, 20]
count ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(temps) - 1
   IF temps[i] > 19 THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT count
```
Output 3. The 19 is not counted because the test is >, not ≥

check.prompt: If the test were changed to `≥ 19`, what would be output?
check.solution: Now 19 counts too: 21, 19, 23, 20, so the output is **4**.

steps.title: Going deeper: the traps examiners set
steps.body:
Three things separate top answers on arrays:

- **Off-by-one**: the last index is `LEN − 1`. A loop that goes to `LEN` reads past the end.
- **Search loops**: a WHILE loop with a `found` flag stops early, but the counter is usually incremented **after** the match, so the final value of `i` is one more than the index found.
- **2D order**: `grid[row][col]`, and nested loops output row by row. Count outputs as rows × columns.

```
nums ← [4, 9, 2, 7]
found ← False
i ← 0
WHILE i < LEN(nums) AND NOT found
   IF nums[i] = 2 THEN
      found ← True
   ENDIF
   i ← i + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT i
```

The 2 is at index 2, but `i` is incremented to 3 before the loop condition is tested again, so the output is 3.

visuals.alt: Trace of the search for 2 in [4, 9, 2, 7]: i 0 and 1 do not match, i 2 matches and sets found to True, i becomes 3 and the condition is then False so the loop stops

check.prompt: In the search program above, the target is changed to 9. What is output?
check.solution: 9 is at index 1. found becomes True and i becomes 2, then the loop stops.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An array holds values of one type, indexed from 0. LEN gives the count; the last index is LEN − 1.
- Traverse with FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(a) − 1. Total, count and biggest all use this loop with a variable set up before it.
- 2D arrays are grids: a[row][col]; nested loops visit row by row. LEN(a) counts the rows and LEN(a[0]) the columns.
- Records group fields of different types; arrays of records store many of them. Reach a field with a dot: pupils[2].name.
- Watch the off-by-one trap and the counter in search loops.

visuals.alt: A table of the four standard array loops, giving for each one the variable set before the loop and the line inside it: a running total, a counter, the biggest so far, and a search

questions.prompt: `items ← ['pen', 'ink', 'pad', 'cap']`. What index does `'pad'` have?
questions.solution: Indexes start at 0: pen is 0, ink is 1, pad is 2.

questions.prompt: What is output by `OUTPUT scores[3]` when `scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]`?
questions.solution: Index 3 is the fourth item, 15.

questions.prompt: What does `LEN(scores)` return for `scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]`?
questions.solution: LEN counts the items. The highest index is one less than LEN.
options: 15, the largest value
4, the number of items
43, the total
3, the highest index

questions.prompt: What is a record?
questions.solution: A record for a student can hold a name (string) and an age (integer) together.
options: A variable that can hold only whole numbers, but any number of them at the same time
A subroutine that saves the values of several variables into a text file at once
A list of values that must all be the same type, stored one after another under one name
A data structure that groups related values of different types under one name, each in a named field

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]
total ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(scores) - 1
   total ← total + scores[i]
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```
questions.solution: 12 + 7 + 9 + 15 = 43. The loop runs for i from 0 to 3.

markScheme.description: Loop adds each of the four items

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program? Give both values in the order they are output, separated by a comma.

```
grid ← [[3, 8, 1],
        [5, 2, 7]]
OUTPUT grid[1][2]
OUTPUT grid[0][1]
```
questions.solution: `grid[1][2]` is row 1, column 2. Row 1 is [5, 2, 7], so that is 7. `grid[0][1]` is row 0, column 1, which is 8. Output 7 then 8. Rows first, then columns, both counted from 0.

questions.prompt: Write code that outputs every item in the array `names` on its own line, whatever its length.
questions.solution: Using LEN, or `FOR name IN names`, is what makes it work for any length. A loop hard-coded to 4 only works for that one array, and the question asks for any length.

markScheme.description: Loop over every item, bounded by LEN or written FOR name IN names
Each item output inside the loop
Correct syntax, and any index starts at 0

criteria.text: A loop that visits every item whatever the length: FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(names) − 1, or FOR name IN names
Outputs each item inside the loop (names[i], or the FOR-IN loop variable)
Correct structure: ENDFOR, and an index, if used, starting at 0

questions.modelAnswer:
```
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(names) - 1
   OUTPUT names[i]
ENDFOR
```

This earns the same marks:

```
FOR name IN names
   OUTPUT name
ENDFOR
```

questions.prompt: Why does the loop in `FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(scores) - 1` stop at `LEN(scores) - 1`?
questions.solution: Four items live at indexes 0, 1, 2, 3. Index 4 is out of range.
options: Because indexes start at 0, the last item is at index LEN − 1; going to LEN would try to read an item that does not exist
Because LEN counts from 1, so the loop has to take one off to match the way the array is stored in memory
Because the first item is not counted by LEN, so the loop has to stop one short to keep the total correct
To make the loop run one extra time at the end, which is needed to add the final item to the total

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
temps ← [18, 21, 19, 23, 20]
count ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(temps) - 1
   IF temps[i] > 19 THEN
      count ← count + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT count
```
questions.solution: Values above 19: 21, 23, 20, so the output is **3**. Note 19 itself is not counted, because the test is > not ≥.

questions.prompt: Write a function `average(nums)` that returns the mean of the values in the array `nums`. You may assume the array is not empty.
questions.skill: writing a function over an array
questions.solution: Total then divide. The divide must use LEN, not a fixed number.

markScheme.description: Loop over every item (LEN(nums) − 1 or FOR n IN nums)
Adds each item to the total

criteria.text: Function header with the array as a parameter
A total variable set to 0 before the loop
A loop over every item (indexed to LEN(nums) − 1, or FOR n IN nums)
Adds each item to the total inside the loop
RETURN total / LEN(nums)
Correct structure and the function does not output

questions.modelAnswer:
```
SUBROUTINE average(nums)
   total ← 0
   FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(nums) - 1
      total ← total + nums[i]
   ENDFOR
   RETURN total / LEN(nums)
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

A loop written `FOR n IN nums` with `total ← total + n` inside earns the same marks.

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
nums ← [4, 9, 2, 7]
found ← False
i ← 0
WHILE i < LEN(nums) AND NOT found
   IF nums[i] = 2 THEN
      found ← True
   ENDIF
   i ← i + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT i
```
questions.solution: The loop finds 2 at index 2 and sets found to True, but i is still incremented to 3 before the WHILE condition is checked again. Output 3.

markScheme.description: 3, because i is incremented after the match

questions.prompt: A program stores 30 students' names, ages and test scores. Which structure is best, and why?
questions.solution: Related values of different types belong in a record; many of them belong in an array of records.
options: Three separate arrays, because an array can only hold one type, and keeping names, ages and scores apart is simpler to write
A 2D array of integers, because scores and ages are numbers
One long array of strings, because every value can be converted to text and read back with STRING_TO_INT when a number is needed
An array of records, one record per student, because each student's different-typed values stay together under one index

questions.prompt:
Complete a trace table for this program, showing `i`, `biggest` and the output.

```
scores ← [12, 7, 9, 15]
biggest ← scores[0]
FOR i ← 1 TO LEN(scores) - 1
   IF scores[i] > biggest THEN
      biggest ← scores[i]
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT biggest
```
questions.solution: Write a row per pass and only change biggest when the IF is true.

criteria.text: biggest starts at 12
i = 1: 7 is not bigger, biggest stays 12; i = 2: 9 is not bigger
i = 3: 15 is bigger, biggest becomes 15
Output 15

questions.modelAnswer:
| i | scores[i] | scores[i] > biggest | biggest | output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   | 12 |   |
| 1 | 7 | False | 12 |   |
| 2 | 9 | False | 12 |   |
| 3 | 15 | True | 15 |   |
|   |   |   |   | 15 |

`biggest` starts as `scores[0]`, which is 12. Only the pass where the IF is True changes it: at `i = 3`, 15 is bigger, so `biggest` becomes 15. After `ENDFOR` the single OUTPUT prints 15.

questions.prompt: `grid` is a 2D array with 4 rows and 6 columns. A program uses nested loops `FOR r ← 0 TO 3` and `FOR c ← 0 TO 5` and outputs `grid[r][c]` each time. How many values are output?
questions.solution: 4 rows × 6 columns = 24. The inner loop runs 6 times for each of the 4 outer passes.

questions.prompt: A record type `Book` has fields `title`, `author` and `pages`. `shelf` is an array of `Book` records. Write the expression that gives the number of pages in the third book on the shelf.
questions.solution: Third book is index 2; then the field with a dot: shelf[2].pages.

questions.prompt:
What is the purpose of this algorithm? `a` is an array of integers.

```
result ← 0
FOR i ← 0 TO LEN(a) - 1
   IF a[i] < 0 THEN
      result ← result + 1
   ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT result
```
questions.skill: determining the purpose of an algorithm
questions.solution: `result` starts at 0 and goes up by **1**, not by `a[i]`, each time the IF is true, so it is a counter: the algorithm counts how many of the values in a are negative. For `[3, -2, 0, -5]` it outputs 2. Adding `a[i]` instead of 1 would make it a total of the negative values, and a finder for the smallest value would start at `a[0]` and replace it.

markScheme.description: Counts how many values are negative

options: It adds up all of the negative values in a
It finds the smallest value that is stored in a
It counts how many of the values in a are negative
It outputs the index of the first negative value

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
grid ← [[4, 1, 6],
        [2, 5, 3]]
grid[1][0] ← grid[0][2] + 1
total ← 0
FOR r ← 0 TO LEN(grid) - 1
   FOR c ← 0 TO LEN(grid[0]) - 1
      total ← total + grid[r][c]
   ENDFOR
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```
questions.solution: `grid[0][2]` is 6, so `grid[1][0]` becomes 6 + 1 = 7 and the grid is now [[4, 1, 6], [7, 5, 3]]. `LEN(grid)` is 2 rows and `LEN(grid[0])` is 3 columns, so the loops add all 6 cells: 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 and 7 + 5 + 3 = 15, which is **26**.

markScheme.description: grid[1][0] becomes 7 before the loops run

questions.prompt: `grid ← [[3, 8, 1], [5, 2, 7]]`. What do `LEN(grid)` and `LEN(grid[0])` return?
questions.solution: `grid` is an array of 2 rows, so `LEN(grid)` is 2. `grid[0]` is the first row, [3, 8, 1], which holds 3 items, so `LEN(grid[0])` is 3, the number of columns. The answer is 2 and 3.
options: 3 and 2, because LEN counts the columns first
6 and 3, because LEN counts every cell in the grid
2 and 3: two rows, then three items in row 0
1 and 2, because LEN gives the last index used

questions.prompt:
A program declares this record and creates a variable:

```
RECORD Car
   make : String
   model : String
   doors : Integer
ENDRECORD

myCar ← Car('Ford', 'Focus', 5)
```

Which line changes the model to `'Fiesta'` and leaves the other fields as they are?
questions.solution: A field is reached through the variable, a dot and the field name, so the line is `myCar.model ← 'Fiesta'`. `Car` is the name of the record type, not a variable, so `Car.model` names no particular car. Fields are reached by name, not by a number in brackets, and `model` on its own would be a new, separate variable.
options: `Car.model ← 'Fiesta'`
`myCar.model ← 'Fiesta'`
`myCar[1] ← 'Fiesta'`
`model ← 'Fiesta'`

questions.solution: Declare the record type once with a type for each field, create a variable from it with the values in the declared order, then reach a field with a dot.

markScheme.description: Record declaration with four named fields (RECORD, or a class, struct or Structure)
Suitable types for all four fields
Variable created with values in field order

criteria.text: A record declaration with the four fields named: RECORD Book … ENDRECORD, or the equivalent in the language used (a Python class or dataclass, a C# struct or class, a VB.NET Structure)
A suitable type for each: title and author String (str, string), pages Integer (int), price Real (float, double or decimal)
Creates the variable with the values in the declared order: b ← Book('River Song', 'A. Patel', 272, 7.99), or b = Book(…) or new Book(…) in a real language
Outputs the field with a dot: OUTPUT b.pages, or print(b.pages), Console.WriteLine(b.pages)

questions.modelAnswer:
```
RECORD Book
   title : String
   author : String
   pages : Integer
   price : Real
ENDRECORD

b ← Book('River Song', 'A. Patel', 272, 7.99)
OUTPUT b.pages
```

The price has a decimal part, so it is a Real; the number of pages is a whole number, so it is an Integer. The values go in the same order as the fields were declared. In Python the same thing is a dataclass with `title: str`, `author: str`, `pages: int` and `price: float`, then `b = Book("River Song", "A. Patel", 272, 7.99)` and `print(b.pages)`; a C# `struct` or VB.NET `Structure` with the same four fields earns the same marks.

questions.prompt: Write a subroutine `gridTotal(grid)` that returns the total of every number in the two-dimensional array of integers `grid`. It must work for a grid with any number of rows and columns; you may assume every row has the same length.
questions.solution: A total set to 0, a loop over the rows, a loop over the columns inside it, add each cell, and return the total after both loops. Bounding the loops with LEN(grid) and LEN(grid[0]), or using FOR-IN, is what makes it work for any size.

markScheme.description: Header with parameter; total ← 0 before the loops
Adds each cell to the total
RETURN total after both loops, no OUTPUT

criteria.text: SUBROUTINE header with the grid as a parameter, and a total set to 0 before the loops
An outer loop over every row: FOR r ← 0 TO LEN(grid) − 1, or FOR row IN grid
An inner loop over every column: FOR c ← 0 TO LEN(grid[0]) − 1 (or LEN(grid[r]) − 1), or FOR x IN row
Adds grid[r][c], or the FOR-IN item, to the total inside the inner loop
RETURN total after both loops have ended, inside SUBROUTINE … ENDSUBROUTINE, with no OUTPUT

questions.modelAnswer:
```
SUBROUTINE gridTotal(grid)
   total ← 0
   FOR r ← 0 TO LEN(grid) - 1
      FOR c ← 0 TO LEN(grid[0]) - 1
         total ← total + grid[r][c]
      ENDFOR
   ENDFOR
   RETURN total
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

This version earns the same marks:

```
SUBROUTINE gridTotal(grid)
   total ← 0
   FOR row IN grid
      FOR x IN row
         total ← total + x
      ENDFOR
   ENDFOR
   RETURN total
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

examTechnique.body: Array questions on Paper 1 are traces (what is output), completions (fill in the missing line), and writing tasks (total, count, find, search). Use LEN in loop bounds, start at 0, and set up the result variable before the loop. For 2D arrays, say row then column. Records can appear as "state a suitable data structure and explain why".
examinerErrors: Starting the index at 1, or looping to LEN instead of LEN − 1.
Forgetting to set total or count to 0 before the loop.
Starting biggest at 0, which fails when all the values are negative; start it at the first item.
Reading a 2D array as column then row.
Using separate arrays where a record, or an array of records, keeps related values together.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses LEN correctly in every loop, traces a search loop to the right final counter value, writes total, count and biggest from memory, handles a 2D array with nested loops in the right order, and can justify a record over parallel arrays.
